name: Design Review

claims.claim_text: Self-checking fails for a specific reason: you skip over what you are certain is right and you see things that are not on the page because they are in your head. That is why even a formal checklist works better when someone else runs it.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can mentally skip over a thing because you, you're 100% sure it's there or you see things that aren't there
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Pull The Trigger

claims.claim_text: Reviewing your own work repeatedly does not converge on the defect that matters. A contractor placed inside an existing engineering team gets review in both directions; the sole engineer at a small company has none, and that absence is a structural risk rather than a matter of diligence.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can come back and review your stuff again and again and not catch the thing that's going to cause the problem
claims.speaker: Alex Klimai
claims.episode_title: More Electronics Consultant Impedance Matching

claims.claim_text: Two engineers working as a team are worth three working separately, because the gain is not extra hours but someone with a different perspective challenging how you interpreted the requirement or the standard.
claims.quote_verbatim: two people working in a team are worth three
claims.speaker: Leigh Brady
claims.episode_title: Siloed Engineering with Leigh Brady

claims.claim_text: The reviewer does not have to be the most knowledgeable person present. A fresh set of eyes is frequently enough on its own to unstick a design, which means the value of a review does not depend on out-ranking the designer technically.
claims.quote_verbatim: just having a fresh set of eyes on things was often enough to get things moving forward again
claims.speaker: Chris Osterwood
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Osterwood

claims.claim_text: Treat checking your own work as impossible and arrange for someone else to do it — a habit worth having even on designs simple enough that the error seems unlikely.
claims.quote_verbatim: your own work is impossible
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Motors And Upgrading Sinclairs - Adapting Apraxiated Automobiles

claims.claim_text: The working form of a review is adversarial but evidenced: the reviewer states that something will not work and gives the reason, and the designer defends it technically by producing the data. A company where that exchange is expected is functioning as intended.
claims.quote_verbatim: the people on the other side of the table are supposed to defend themselves technically
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Design Reviews Are Important - Habitual Hype Hebetude

claims.claim_text: An objection has to carry its reason with it. Saying only that something will not work gives the designer nothing to answer and turns a technical disagreement into a personal one.
claims.quote_verbatim: just say, it's not going to work because
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Distribution, Wozniak & Robots - Early Eight-bit Endgame

claims.claim_text: Circulate readable schematics on paper before the meeting. Asking a room to navigate to page four of a PDF does not work, and reviewers need to be able to mark up and cross-reference pages simultaneously.
claims.quote_verbatim: schematics that are already printed out
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Distribution, Wozniak & Robots - Early Eight-bit Endgame

claims.claim_text: Arrive with the evidence rather than the conclusion: datasheets, test reports and everything generated during the design. The reviewers' questions will range across whatever they know, and the material you cannot produce in the room becomes the open item.
claims.quote_verbatim: walked in with a, probably a stack of papers, data sheets, test reports, everything I've generated
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ryan Brown - Effortless Equipment Extensibility

claims.claim_text: A rigorous review serves two purposes at once — catching the defect and teaching the engineer how to design, test, evaluate and document — which is why organisations that treat it as pure quality control get less out of it than they could.
claims.quote_verbatim: only do we want the product to be very high quality, but it's part of the way that we teach engineers
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ryan Brown - Effortless Equipment Extensibility

claims.claim_text: Almost nobody enjoys being reviewed, and the durable way through is to enter each one intending to learn at least one thing, which makes the time productive regardless of how the design fares.
claims.quote_verbatim: the way to get
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ryan Brown - Effortless Equipment Extensibility

claims.claim_text: Timing matters as much as content. Being interrupted mid-schematic with a list of alternatives you have already tried and rejected is corrosive, because you then have to prove the negative; presenting a finished holistic view and defending it is the exchange that actually works.
claims.quote_verbatim: want to get to the end and then have a design review where you can say, here is the holistic view
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Processors, CEOs & Soldering irons - Plentiful Perfunctory Programs

claims.claim_text: Rules of thumb earn their place in the review room: with ten people around a design on the wall, the question is whether this is going to work or whether you are in the danger zone, and nobody is going to run a field solver to find out. Fast approximation is what lets a group explore the design space at the whiteboard.
claims.quote_verbatim: you don't want to take the time to run over and run your 3D field solver
claims.speaker: Eric Bogatin
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Eric Bogatin - Tilded Thumb Tenets

claims.claim_text: A review answers a different question from a rule check. Automated checking asks whether something can be done; a reviewer asks whether it should — the protection diode that solves one problem and creates three is exactly the kind of thing no rule set flags.
claims.quote_verbatim: you put in this ESD diode to solve a problem, but maybe it's going to cause three other problems
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Hardware Revision Control with Kyle Dumont

claims.claim_text: An outside review of customer designs repeatedly found large fractions — in one case forty percent — that could simply be deleted, on cost and on power. The diagnostic question is why each block is present, and the revealing answer is silence.
claims.quote_verbatim: 40% of your design is not really required
claims.speaker: Pallav Aggarwal
claims.episode_title: Blogging Electronics with Pallav Aggarwal

claims.claim_text: A domestic appliance failed after ten years because its designers ran resistors far too hot — a mistake five minutes of review would have caught, and one whose cost lands on the owner as a heavy, expensive product scrapped for a component worth cents.
claims.quote_verbatim: it all comes down to a rookie mistake that a five-minute design review would have been like, you can't do that
claims.speaker: Dave Young
claims.episode_title: Two Dads Puzzlin Things Out

claims.claim_text: Insufficient scrutiny shows up first in mechanical safety rather than in electronics: a multi-pound spinning disc retained by a single grub screw on a motor shaft is the kind of decision that survives only because nobody senior looked at it.
claims.quote_verbatim: there wasn't enough scrutiny on the design to say, well, it's probably not a good idea to like suspend this disc
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Mike Harrison - X-ray Examining Xenogogue

claims.claim_text: When a product fails on something as calculable as write endurance, only two explanations remain: nobody ran the numbers, or somebody did and was not willing to say so. Both are review-culture failures rather than technical ones, and the second is the more serious.
claims.quote_verbatim: if an engineer spoke up at a meeting and said, Hey, look, I've, I've ran the numbers
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: KonnectorPanik

claims.claim_text: Schedule pressure on a first custom board strips out testability first — no test points, no broken-out debug channel — and the result is a board that gives no information at all when it fails to boot. The time saved by not fanning out a test interface is reliably smaller than the time then spent guessing.
claims.quote_verbatim: these boards just have like no testability, right? Like there's no test points on the things
claims.speaker: Charles Aylward
claims.episode_title: Software for Rockets with Charles Aylward

claims.claim_text: Add one question to the review agenda: when this board comes back and does not work, how will we find out why? Answering it before fabrication is what puts the test points on the board, and buying a third-party review is a reasonable substitute where the team is too small to hold one.
claims.quote_verbatim: make, design review a thing and sit down and do the process of like, okay, well once this comes in and it doesn't work, how do we test it
claims.speaker: Charles Aylward
claims.episode_title: Software for Rockets with Charles Aylward

claims.claim_text: Substituting a passive on its headline parameters — capacitance, package, voltage — misses the ones buried deeper in the catalogue, such as dielectric technology or tolerance. Exhaustive automated comparison removes the dependence on how thorough the reviewer happened to be that day.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's a different capacitor technology or it's different tolerance
claims.speaker: Michael
claims.episode_title: Product Lifecycle Management with Michael Corr

claims.claim_text: Process rigour has acquired a bad name next to lighter-weight methods, but it makes the project faster overall: slower at the start, with a crossover point after which the accumulated rework of the fast approach exceeds it.
claims.quote_verbatim: this sort of like more rigorous approaches actually make you go faster
claims.speaker: Charles Aylward
claims.episode_title: Software for Rockets with Charles Aylward

claims.claim_text: First-time-right designs are the visible end of front-loaded work — months of evaluation and repeated review — rather than evidence of a better designer. Anyone claiming it without that investment is describing a small delta revision, not a new design.
claims.quote_verbatim: says first time right design, they have done more work towards, you know, reviews and, you know, evaluation
claims.speaker: Pallav Aggarwal
claims.episode_title: Blogging Electronics with Pallav Aggarwal

claims.claim_text: The time spent checking before fabrication is the cheapest time in the project, and the expectation to hold is that you will get something wrong regardless — checking changes how much, not whether.
claims.quote_verbatim: get it right double triple quadruple check it because you are going to get it wrong no matter what
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: EE Movies, Part Rants and SPICE.

claims.claim_text: Skipping design work up front produces visible early progress and an unverifiable result: work written to get something running quickly becomes tangled enough that it is thrown out and restarted, and the apparent speed is repaid with interest.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can make it look like you're getting a lot of progress done, but when it comes down to verifying all this sloppy code
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - The Ternary Tussle

claims.claim_text: Practice only compounds where feedback closes the loop, so an hour of layout followed by a colleague telling you what is wrong with it counts and an hour of unreviewed work does not. This makes review the mechanism by which experience becomes skill rather than repetition.
claims.quote_verbatim: an hour of practice only counts if you're actually getting feedback
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Project Management, Lasers & Robots - Staunch Specialty Sanctanimity

claims.claim_text: Some organisations staff a second team purely to look over the shoulders of the first, formally and informally, as a standing culture of peer review. It works, and it is contentious — professional rivalries do not disappear because the process is professional.
claims.quote_verbatim: a team of really smart people kind of looking over the shoulders of the people who are kind of working on the program
claims.speaker: Kent Lundberg
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dr. Kent Lundberg - Luculent Linear Legacy

claims.claim_text: A workable model for collaborative hardware is one designer making substantial changes with two or three others acting as sounding board, reviewer and architecture help. It depends on the design tool using a text-based file format, because otherwise revision control cannot support the conversation.
claims.quote_verbatim: one person is a designer and other people are there to help that designer
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Interview with Michael Ossmann - Gifted Grimgribber Grokker

claims.claim_text: The pull request is the software world's design review: a branch carrying the proposed changes, opened for comment before it merges. Bringing that pattern to hardware requires only that the tooling can show what changed between two versions.
claims.quote_verbatim: basically the Git equivalent of a design review
claims.speaker: Kyle Dumont
claims.episode_title: Hardware Revision Control with Kyle Dumont

claims.claim_text: A reviewer from the adjacent discipline catches a distinct class of error — a firmware engineer reviewing a schematic sees the consequences of pin assignment and boot configuration that the hardware designer has stopped noticing.
claims.quote_verbatim: he's fixed a lot of my schematics over the years
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: This Is Just A Tribute

claims.claim_text: A standing meeting of fifteen to twenty specialists discussing problems in their own domain is an unmatched teaching environment, and it is the thing an engineer entering a small company gives up without necessarily realising it.
claims.quote_verbatim: would have a meeting like with like 15 to 20 analog engineers in a room just talking about analog topics
claims.speaker: Philip Salmony
claims.episode_title: Mixed Signal Education with Philip Salmony

claims.claim_text: Outside an organisation the guardrails have to be built deliberately: mentorship has to be sought out and design reviews have to be paid for, which is a real cost that people leaving structured employers routinely fail to budget.
claims.quote_verbatim: you pay for design reviews. You just have to work harder
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Siloed Engineering with Leigh Brady

claims.claim_text: Designing where others can watch the process rather than only the result improves quality directly, because knowing the work is visible changes how carefully it is done and makes the team more receptive to feedback than designing in a vacuum ever does.
claims.quote_verbatim: the more that you design out in the open, I think it actually improves the quality of the product
claims.speaker: Brian Faith
claims.episode_title: Open FPGA Toolchains and Machine Learning with Brian Faith of QuickLogic

claims.claim_text: Internal peer review is also how invention disclosures are filtered before they reach a patent attorney: a design community says either that the idea was done a decade ago or that it has legs, which is far cheaper than finding out from a patent examiner.
claims.quote_verbatim: we would have like a design community look at it first
claims.speaker: Dafydd Roche
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Dafydd Roche

claims.claim_text: Engineers are sometimes required to defend a design they did not choose and do not believe in. The failure mode that follows is predictable — the specification gets massaged, or the results do — and the review has then been converted into theatre.
claims.quote_verbatim: you've been given a shit design. You've got to design it, and you hate the design
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Distribution, Wozniak & Robots - Early Eight-bit Endgame

claims.claim_text: Having your reasoning heard, considered and overruled is a legitimate outcome of a review. Being ignored and told not to rock the boat is a different thing entirely, and it is reasonable to read it as information about the employer rather than about the design.
claims.quote_verbatim: when they just ignore you and tell you to shut up and go in the corner
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Is This A Show?

claims.claim_text: Cost is a standing participant in every review of a high-volume product: the part that would obviously improve the design is frequently the part the bill of materials cannot carry, and that constraint is not a failure of engineering ambition.
claims.quote_verbatim: it'd be nice to have one of these chips here, you can't afford it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Senseless Saccadic Shemozzle

claims.claim_text: On compressed silicon schedules the board work starts before the pinout is finalised, with layout and applications engineers engaged from the outset and schematic capture proceeding in parallel with tape-out. The schematic and layout reviews still happen; what changes is that they happen against a moving target.
claims.quote_verbatim: you want your PCB layout guys involved. You want your applications engineers guys involved
claims.speaker: Kieran O'Leary
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Kieran O'Leary

claims.claim_text: Bringing up untested silicon usually means a custom socket so parts can be swapped, and those sockets run into thousands of dollars — a cost that belongs in the schedule discussion early, because the test programme cannot be validated without physical samples.
claims.quote_verbatim: those sockets can run to thousands of dollars
claims.speaker: Kieran O'Leary
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Kieran O'Leary

claims.claim_text: A schematic that flows left to right, with well-named components and notes describing intent, is reviewable in a way that a hundred-page binder with one net per page is not. Good architecture documents itself to a degree, and the point at which a design stops being self-explanatory is usually the point at which it was bent to do something it was not designed for.
claims.quote_verbatim: a schematic where it kind of flows left to right and components are, have notes
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer
claims.episode_title: Wait, why is Jeff glowing?

claims.claim_text: Hand over the reasoning, not just the design: which constraints applied, why a circuit looks odd, and honestly which parts you would do differently now. That lets the next engineer build on the work instead of rediscovering the same dead ends, and it is far more useful than any volume of after-the-fact documentation.
claims.quote_verbatim: not just what it did, but sort of what the decisions that were made
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer
claims.episode_title: Wait, why is Jeff glowing?

claims.claim_text: Circulating a board for checking before fabrication is worth doing even with reviewers less experienced than you, because enthusiasm produces methodical component-by-component checking that an expert skims past.
claims.quote_verbatim: did you give this board out to people before you got it fabbed and asked them to check it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Cheap Respins And A Time Machine - Multiscience Mercenary Marketplace

claims.claim_text: A review of someone else's design starts before the schematic: existing documentation, any competitive analysis, and the reason the thing is being built at all. Without the intent, a reviewer can only check consistency, not suitability.
claims.quote_verbatim: your links to your existing documentation, competitive analysis, whatever, you know, reason why you're doing what you're doing
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Monster Scale Production

claims.claim_text: Automatically generated schematics split along a familiar axis: generating from datasheet data covers anything but produces work that must be reviewed carefully, while assembling manufacturer-supplied blocks known to work covers less ground with much higher assurance, leaving only the connections between blocks to check.
claims.quote_verbatim: you have a much greater assurance that what you are generating is actually going to be correct because you're taking blocks of working circuitry
claims.speaker: Zachariah Peterson
claims.episode_title: Layout Review with Zachariah Peterson

attribution_notes: attribution_reliable was not trusted. ep138 (Ryan Brown), ep425 (Chris Osterwood), ep584 (Charles Aylward), ep577 (Michael Corr) and ep505 (Kyle Dumont) label host questions with the guest's name; claims were assigned by content and only material unambiguously the guest's own was used.
ep116's exchange about handling difficult reviewers is heavily profane in the original; the claims keep the substance — objections must carry reasons — without the wording.
ep170's discussion of whether attending design reviews makes someone an engineer is about job titles rather than review practice, and was excluded.
Host banter about disliking meetings, company politics and individual colleagues was excluded as non-transferable.
